work.title: Der wundervolle Tod des Welterlösers. Ein Oratorium

history.p:
In 1749 after Scheibe had been pensioned as Kapellmeister, he and his family decided to move to Sønderborg in the southern part of Denmark where they established a music school for children. Scheibe also supplemented his pension by translating mainly academic studies for the publishers Franz Christian Mumme. However, he retained contact with the musical environment in Copenhagen and was an important instigator of the newly established musical society as well as an active participant in their concerts and had new works performed. Though he did not compose as much as earlier, one of the works which he did write is the present Passion oratorio; he also wrote the text himself. The first version of the libretto was finished in 1754, and since he was living in Sønderborg he had it issued by Korte in Altona and Flensburg, a publishing house that he had used a couple of times before. Apparently the work remained unperformed for seven years, that is until he returned to Copenhagen. In the published libretto of 1754, Scheibe includes an extensive introduction and discussion of the genre. He criticises the traditional approach to the framework of the Passion oratorio according to which the evangelist’s prose is placed between the arias and recitatives. Scheibe’s approach to the genre is based entirely on the dramatic sense and begins with darkness which arose in the sixth hour and continues until Jesus’ death. The characters of the oratorio are Jesus, Mary, John, Lazarus, Eidli, the people, women, and the believers, among others. Lazarus and Eidli are characters most likely inspired by Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock’s ‘Messias’ (published between 1748 and 1773), also noted by the reviewer of Fortgesetzte Nachrichten (1758). It was in the early 1760s that Scheibe and Klopstock discussed aspects of setting music to texts and Scheibe published several articles dealing with the recitative. The present oratorio is thus part of Scheibe’s experiment to transform his ideas from theory to compositional practice.
In the second edition of the text book which appeared in 1761, Scheibe explains that he had set the text to music some time ago; since it was to be performed and the libretto to be sold to the audience, he decided to revise it adding and changing some details. Thus he added an extra aria for the 'Hauptmann' and changed a few sections of the character's recitatives in the first part of the oratorio (nos. 11–13). The first performance took place during Lent 1761, on Sunday 8 March. However, with more than thirty sections the work was so large that its performance was divided over two evenings; in all, it was performed four times. According to the newspapers, the oratorio did not receive its first performance in The Musical Society but in the town residence of Frederik Raben (1693–1773), who was one of Scheibe’s protectors and patrons. Each winter, and until 1766–67, the Raben family stayed in Copenhagen for around five months, participating in the court life. According to the diary of Frederik’s son, Otto Ludvig, he played at the event or at least at one of the rehearsals (‘Repet.’). The event attracted large audiences.
A positive review of the libretto appeared already in 1758 in the journal Fortgesetzte Nachrichten mentioning among other things that 'in the foreword placed at the beginning, the author introduces his thoughts on Passion music with his usual force of evaluation. He reproaches those who mix the prosaic narrative of evangelist in the arias etc. The structure of his "Singgedicht" is quite dramatic. Thus he has not included all the circumstances regarding the Passion but only those that he actually considered relevant for his purpose. The plot begins at the darkness which occurred at the sixth hour and continues until the death of Jesus.' The reviewer concludes that 'this “Singgedicht” is, moreover, very well composed and has a marked advantage over the preceding one [i.e. SchW B2:300?].'
Only the first part of the Passion oratorio has survived. It was obtained by the music collector Georg Poelchau in Berlin, possibly from Scheibe's estate and possibly with the help of his connections in Copenhagen which included C.E.F. Weyse. Later the city wait of Flensburg, O.J.C. Timmermann (1717–1800) composed a new cantata based on Scheibe's text. This work was performed in 1778 in Flensburg; however, only a printed libretto seems to have survived (DK-Kk, 4,-429, 8o).

annot.p: 'Der Herr Verfasser eröffnet in dem vorangesetzten Vorbericht seine Gedanken über die Paßionsmusiken, mit seiner gewöhnlichen Beurtheilungskraft. Er tadelt diejenigen billig in welche die prosaische Erzählung des Evangelisten unter die Arien &c. gemischt wird. Die Einrichtung seines Singgedichtes ist ganz dramatisch. Er hat dabey nicht alle Umstände der Leidensgeschichte mitgenommen, sondern nur die, welche er seinem Endzweck eigentlich gemäß zu seyn erachtet hat. Die Handlung fängt von der Finsterniß die um die sechste Stunde geschahe, an, und dauert bis auf den Tod Jesu. [...] Uebrigen ist dieses Singgedicht sehr wohl abgefasset und hat einen merklichen Vorzug vor den vorhergehenden.'

A concert in which a complete new passion oratorio by Scheibe will be performed; it consists of two parts and will be performed at four subscription concerts. Tickets and booklets are obtainable from Scheibe and the first performance will take place at Raben's old residence in 'Stormgaden'.

incipText.p: Wo sind wir?
Wer du auch seyst, den man dort angeheftet hat
O! tödtet mich nur auch, vermeßne Schaaren!
Ach Heiland! Sohn! ach tröste mich!
Du Herrscher über Tod und Leben!
Wie liebenswürdig sind die Triebe
Fließt, zitternde Thränen, entdecket mein Leiden!
Doch Herz! von manchen Wiedersprüchen voll!
O! matter Trost bey so viel Kummer!
Selge Hoffnung! wie stärkst du die Glieder!
Was für ein Volk ist das?

annot.p: A section of the present recitative has been expanded and another has been shortened (see also Scheibe's foreword to the printed libretto (1761)).

incipText.p: Wo bin ich? Was rühret mich?

annot.p: The present aria has been added in the second version of the oratorio (1761); see also Scheibe's foreword to the printed libretto.

incipText.p: Doch träum ich? – wird es Tag? Hilf Himmel! welcher Schein!

annot.p: Part of the present recitative (Der Hauptmann) has been added to the revised edition of the oratorio in 1761; see also Scheibe's foreword to the libretto (1761).

incipText.p: Was für Martern, was für Plagen
Mich dürstet!
Du wirst, o Herr! für unsre Sünden

annot.p: As the music has not survived, the sections are taken from the printed libretto of 1761.

incipText.p: O! Wunder! seht, der HErr erhohlet sich!
Meine Lieben, gute Nacht!
O Gott! o Ruf! durchdringendes Geschrey!
Entflieht! entflieht! die Welt vergeht!
Es mag die Welt zertrümmern und vergehn
Wie selig! daß wir hoffen können
Wenn alle Elemente krachen
Gekreuzigter! Ich deiner Gottheit Bekenner
Entsetzliche Verändrung der Natur!
Beleidigter Richter! Messias! erwache! –
Undankbar Volk! wird nun dein Gott erkannt?
Ach! da dieß Volk verzweifelnd zagt
Ach! Zion! ach, wie tief bist du gebeugt!
Ach! ist der Anblick zu ertragen?
Ihr Lieben! die ihr hier vor Thränen
Ihr heiligen, erblaßten Glieder!
Mich auch, mich stärkt ein neues Licht
Bald werden wir Ihn lebend sehen
O! Trost! der auch in unsre Herzen fließet
Der Tag soll ewig heilig seyn!

titlePage.p: <Eigenhändige Partitur des Componisten. [= Poelchau]> | Der wundervolle | Tod des Welterlösers. | Ein | Oratorium. | Poesie und Musik | von | J. A. Scheiben. | Erster Theil.

physDesc.watermark: emblem consisting of a coat-of-arms with a single diagonal band and the fleur-de-lis and the countermark 'IV' or 'VI' is partly visible. The same watermark is also seen in SchW B2:301 and B2:431 suggesting that all three works were most likely produced around the same time. Paper of a dense and rather coarse quality meaning that it is difficult to draw staves on the paper.
physDesc.physMedium: In 2o; upright format, consisting of 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2 nested bifolios; title page (fol. 1r), list of instruments, characters and choirs (fol. 1v), music (fols. 2r–62v; numbered 5–126 in ink (Scheibe)); in all 62 folios. Hand-ruled paper, between 18 and 20 staves (7 mm; single rastrum used) in dark brown ink and music in same ink; most top and bottom staves have not been used. A clean autograph ink fair copy with very few changes. Same source type as D-B, Scheibe 1a and Scheibe 3. As the new sections of 1761 are found in the score, it must therefore be a later (revised?) version and not the early one. The score only includes the first part; apparently the second has been lost.

In original grey limp binding (same as D-B, Scheibe 1a, 3) with raised bands and yellow label 'Scheibe’s Tod Jesu | Partitur.' presumably in Poelchau's hand pasted on spine; above '11.' added in ink, perhaps contemporary with Scheibe; pasted on end paste-down is the ex libris 'Ex | bibliotheca | Poelchavian.' A modern label has been pasted on front cover. The binding must indeed be original as in two sources (the present one and D-B, Scheibe 1b) the paste-down includes staves which are in the same ink of of the same size as the rest of the manuscript.
